l: Hello and welcome to Digital Tech Revision, the podcast for CCEA GCSE Digital Technology. I'm Aoife.
And I'm Conor. Today's episode is lesson L14: CPU performance and memory: RAM, ROM and cache.
So Conor, if someone only remembers one thing from today, what should it be?
Explain how clock speed, cache size and number of cores each affect CPU performance. That is the heart of it.
Okay, take us through it properly.

The performance of a CPU means how quickly it can carry out instructions. The CCEA specification names three factors. The first is clock speed. The CPU contains a clock that sends out regular pulses, and the clock speed is the number of fetch to execute cycles the CPU can carry out each second. It is measured in hertz, and modern processors are measured in gigahertz: a 3 gigahertz processor can perform three billion cycles per second.
Makes sense. Keep going.

The second factor is the number of cores. A core is a full processing unit: each one has a control unit, an ALU and a set of registers, so a quad-core processor can work on four instructions at the same time. The third factor is cache size. Cache is a small amount of very fast memory close to the CPU that holds frequently used instructions and data. When choosing a computer for a task, such as gaming or editing video, all three should be considered together, along with the amount of RAM.
Right. What else do we need to know?

A higher clock speed means more instructions are processed each second, but it also produces more heat and uses more battery power. Also, if the other parts of the computer cannot supply data quickly enough, the CPU ends up waiting, so doubling the clock speed does not double the overall speed. In the same way, more cores only help if the software has been written to split its work into parts that can run in parallel. A simple program that does one thing at a time may use only one core, and the others sit idle.
Got it. Keep going.

More cores are very useful when several programs are open, or for jobs that split up easily, such as rendering video. A larger cache means the CPU finds what it needs in the cache more often. Each time it does, it avoids a slower trip to RAM, so processing is faster. However, cache is expensive to make, which is why it is kept small.
And is there anything people often mix up here?

Internal memory is memory the CPU can access directly. Random access memory (RAM) is the main memory. Its purpose is to hold the operating system, programs and data that are currently in use, such as a web browser and the page you are reading. RAM can be read from and written to, and its contents change all the time. It is volatile, meaning everything in it is lost when the power is switched off, which is why files must be saved to storage.
Okay. Keep going.

Read only memory (ROM) can be read but not normally changed. It is non-volatile, so it keeps its contents without power. Its purpose is to store the boot program, the instructions the computer needs as soon as it is switched on. Cache is the third type. Like RAM it can be read from and written to and it is volatile, but it is much smaller and much faster, and it sits inside or right beside the CPU.
Go on.

When you press the power button, RAM is empty, so the computer cannot start from it. Instead, the CPU runs the start-up instructions stored in ROM, often called the BIOS. These instructions check that key hardware is working and then load the operating system from the hard disc or SSD into RAM. Once the operating system is in RAM, it takes over. While the computer is running, RAM can fill up if many programs are open.
Right. Keep going.

The operating system then uses part of the storage drive as extra memory, called virtual memory, moving data that is not being used right now out of RAM. Because storage drives are much slower than RAM, the computer slows down as data is swapped back and forth. This is why adding more RAM can make a computer faster: it reduces the need for virtual memory. The textbook says larger RAM makes the processor faster; more precisely, it stops the processor having to wait for slow storage.
Time for quickfire key terms. I'll say the term, and you give me the answer the mark scheme gives credit for.
Go for it.
Clock speed?
The number of fetch to execute cycles a CPU can carry out per second, measured in hertz (e dot g. 3 gigahertz equals 3 billion cycles per second).
Core?
An independent processing unit inside a CPU; each core has a control unit, an ALU and registers, so it can process instructions at the same time as other cores.
Cache?
Small, very fast memory on or near the CPU that holds frequently used instructions and data, so they need not be fetched from slower RAM.
RAM?
Random access memory: volatile read/write main memory that holds the operating system, programs and data currently in use.
ROM?
Read only memory: non-volatile memory whose contents cannot normally be changed, used to store the boot-up instructions (BIOS).
Volatile?
Describes memory that loses its contents when the power is switched off, such as RAM and cache.
What about the exam? Where has this come up?

Performance and memory questions appear often. Clock speed and its units came up in the 2021 paper, question 5 and the 2022 paper, question 12. RAM and ROM have been tested in the 2019 paper, question 5 and the 2024 paper, question 6, and ROM's role in booting appeared in the 2025 paper, question 4. Cache came up in the 2024 paper, question 5 and as a matching term in the 2025 paper, question 13. For 'describe the impact' questions, give the cause and the effect: 'a higher clock speed means more fetch to execute cycles per second, so more instructions are processed per second'. For cache, the marks usually need two ideas: it is faster to access than RAM, and it holds frequently used data or instructions. For RAM versus ROM, give a matched pair of differences, such as 'RAM is volatile but ROM is non-volatile', rather than describing only one memory. Common mistakes are saying clock speed is measured in bytes, saying ROM holds the user's files, and saying that cache is part of the hard disc.

Let's finish with a question for the listeners. Why does a larger cache usually improve performance? Is it A, It increases the clock speed; B, It adds more cores; C, More frequently used data is kept close to the CPU, so there are fewer slow trips to RAM; D, It stores the operating system permanently?
I'll give you a few seconds.
The answer is C: More frequently used data is kept close to the CPU, so there are fewer slow trips to RAM. Cache is faster than RAM, so the more the CPU can find there, the less time it waits.
